failures.title: Aston Martin AE31DBS Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Ignition Coil Degradation - 30,000-60,000 miles
items.whatHappens: The AE31DBS's ignition coil packs are mounted directly on top of the spark plugs in the V12's valley. The heat from the twin turbos bakes the coil packs over time, causing them to fail. The first symptom is usually a misfire under load, accompanied by a CEL. According to Aston Martin specialist Bamford Rose, "most if not all V12's will suffer coil failure at some point causing misfire". Poorly protected coil packs leading to misfires and spark plug corrosion are recognised issues.
items.repairVsReplace: Coil pack replacement requires removing the intake plenum and is labour-intensive. Specialists recommend replacing all 12 coil packs and spark plugs as preventative maintenance at 50,000 miles. Budget £2,000-£3,500 for the full job.

items.title: Breather Valve Sticking - 40,000-80,000 miles
items.whatHappens: All V12-engined Aston Martins can suffer from sticking breather valves, causing "oil pullover and likely misfire". When the breather valve sticks, excessive crankcase pressure forces oil into the intake system, leading to misfires and potential catalytic converter damage. In severe cases, "failure which puts at risk the cat which in turn can cause catastrophic engine failure".
items.repairVsReplace: Breather valve replacement is a standard but important maintenance item. If caught early, replacement costs £500-£1,000. If the issue has caused catalytic converter damage, costs escalate significantly.

items.title: Cooling System Leaks - 40,000-80,000 miles
items.whatHappens: The AE31DBS produces significant heat - 715-770 bhp from 5.2 litres requires sophisticated cooling. The water-to-air charge coolers and associated plumbing can develop leaks over time. The V12's all-aluminium construction means it does not tolerate overheating.
items.repairVsReplace: Cooling system component replacement is labour-intensive due to engine bay packaging. Budget £1,500-£3,000 for a comprehensive cooling system refresh.

failures.goodYearsLine: The AE31DBS is considered a robust and well-engineered engine when properly maintained. According to PistonHeads, "the AE31 is an extremely well engineered and robust engine" featuring "high quality forged crank, forged rods and forged pistons". Most issues are ancillaries rather than fundamental engine failures.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the AE31DBS
variants.intro: The AE31DBS is the high-output variant of Aston Martin's 5.2-litre twin-turbo V12, producing 715-770 bhp and 900 Nm of torque. It features a 60° V12 configuration with 48 valves, all-alloy construction, and water-to-air charge cooling. Where to find your engine code: The engine code is stamped on the block - typically on a machined pad near the front of the engine. The code is listed as AE31 on technical documentation. It also appears on your V5C logbook. Commonly confused codes: - AE31 (DB11 V12) - the 600-630 bhp version used in the DB11; shares the same block but has different ECU calibration, lower boost and lower output - AM28 6.0L V12 - the naturally aspirated 6.0L V12 used in the previous generation DBS and DB9; completely different engine, no turbos - M177 4.0L V8 - the Mercedes-AMG V8 used in Aston Martin's V8 lineup; entirely different engine family Why fitting the wrong revision matters: The AE31DBS was produced in multiple power tunes - 715 bhp (DBS Superleggera), 725 PS (715 bhp), and 770 PS (759 bhp, 770 Ultimate). The DBS 770 Ultimate produces 770 PS (759 bhp) and 900 Nm of torque. The ECU calibration, boost pressure, fuel injectors and cooling system all differ between tunes. Fitting the wrong spec will result in incorrect fuelling, boost control and potentially engine damage.

relatives.description: AE31 (DB11 V12): - the standard 5.2L twin-turbo V12 that debuted in the DB11 V12, producing 600-630 bhp. The AE31DBS is a significantly higher-output evolution - 715-770 bhp - with increased boost, upgraded intercooling, and more aggressive ECU calibration.

edition DBS 770 Ultimate (2023-2024) uses the same AE31DBS engine but produces 770 PS (759 bhp) - the most powerful Aston Martin V12 ever fitted to a production car. It features bespoke calibration and upgraded internals.

hybrid (48V) version of the AE31 family is expected in future V12 applications, using the same block and turbos but adding a starter-generator and small battery pack. An engine page is pending for this variant.

M177 4.0L V8: - Aston Martin's V8 alternative, used in the V8 Vantage, DB11 V8 and DBX. It is not related mechanically to the AE31DBS, but many buyers cross-shop the two. The M177 is considerably cheaper to replace (from £8,000) but lacks the V12's character and exclusivity.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement AE31DBS - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used AE31DBS makes sense only with full documented service history and evidence that the coil packs, breather valves and cooling system have been addressed. Given the high value of the cars these engines sit in, a used engine with known history can be a viable option, but the risk of inheriting someone else's problems is real - especially with the known coil and breather valve issues. Specialist inspection is essential. Used engines guide

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper AE31DBS recon addresses the ignition coil packs, breather valves, cooling system components, turbo oil feed lines and all common wear items. Reconditioned units from vetted UK specialists come with a 12-24 month warranty and are the default choice for most DBS Superleggera owners. At £18,000-£24,000 supply-only, they offer the best balance of cost and peace of mind for a flagship V12 car. Reconditioned engines guide

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full rebuild is justified for high-value collectable examples (DBS 770 Ultimate, low-mileage Superleggera) or where the original engine has matching-numbers value. A proper AE31DBS rebuild should include a full bottom-end rebuild, new turbochargers, upgraded cooling system, and all ancillaries. Budget £24,000-£30,000+ for a specialist rebuild. Rebuilt engines guide

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All three options can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted UK Aston Martin V12 specialists, with warranties backed by the fitting workshop. Nationwide delivery and fit available. Supply & fit guide
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The AE31DBS sits exclusively in vehicles worth £150,000-£400,000+. A reconditioned engine at £18,000-£24,000 represents 4-12% of the vehicle's value, making replacement financially viable across the entire range. The DBS Superleggera's high value means even the most expensive rebuilt option is justified. That said, given the significant investment, full due diligence - including specialist inspection and thorough service history review - is essential before any purchase decision.

items.question: What is the most common problem with the Aston Martin AE31DBS engine?
items.answer: Ignition coil degradation is the most common issue - the V12's heat bakes the coil packs, causing misfires. Specialists recommend replacing all 12 coil packs and spark plugs at 50,000 miles as preventative maintenance. Breather valve sticking and cooling system leaks are also reported. Coil pack replacement (all 12): £2,000-£3,500. Breather valve replacement: £500-£1,000. Cooling system overhaul: £1,500-£3,000.

items.question: Which Aston Martin models use the AE31DBS engine?
items.answer: The AE31DBS powers the DBS Superleggera (2018-2024), DBS Superleggera Volante (2019-2024), and the limited-edition DBS 770 Ultimate (2023-2024). It is the high-output variant of the AE31 V12, producing 715-770 bhp. [See full compatibility list above]

items.question: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or rebuilt AE31DBS engine?
items.answer: For most owners, a reconditioned AE31DBS with new coil packs, breather valves and cooling system overhaul is the best balance of cost and reliability. Used: only with full service history and specialist inspection. Reconditioned: default for DBS Superleggera owners, 12-24 month warranty. items.question: How do I know if my Aston Martin has the AE31DBS engine?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on a machined pad near the front of the engine. The AE31DBS is the 5.2L twin-turbo V12 that powers the DBS Superleggera and 770 Ultimate. items.question: What's the difference between the AE31DBS and the standard AE31?
items.answer: The AE31DBS is the high-output evolution of the AE31. It features higher boost pressure, upgraded intercooling, and more aggressive ECU calibration to produce 715-770 bhp (vs 600-630 bhp in the DB11 V12). The core block, turbos and V12 architecture are the same, but the calibration and ancillaries differ significantly. [Read about the AE31DBS development]
